'''Clara Franzini-Armstrong''' (born on 3 October 1938) is an [[Electron microscope|electron microscopist]]<ref name=Biophysicists-2>{{cite journal|title=Biophysicists in Profile: Clara Franzini-Armstrong|journal=The Biophysics Society Newsletter|date=August 2009}}</ref> and [[professor emerita]] of [[Cell biology|cell]] and [[developmental biology]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].<ref name=ClaraPhD-4>{{cite journal|title=Clara Franzini-Armstrong, Ph.D. Cell and Developmental Biology; Faculty and Administration|journal=Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania|date=14 August 2008}}</ref><ref name="Welcome-9">{{cite journal|title=Welcome to The Pennsylvania Muscle Institute|journal=Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania|date=14 August 2008}}</ref>

==Early life==

Franzini-Armstrong was born in [[Florence]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Penn’s 2017 Commencement Speaker and Honorary Degree Recipients |url=https://almanac.upenn.edu/articles/penns-2017-commencement-speaker-and-honorary-degree-recipients |access-date=2025-11-04 |website=almanac.upenn.edu |language=en}}</ref> on 3 October 1938. She lived with both of her parents along with her brothers Paolo, Carlo, and Marco. Her father was an [[Atomic physics|atomic physicist]], and her mother had a physics degree. She became interested in science during her schooling.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Fondazione Onda ETS |url=https://fondazioneonda.it/it/pubblicazione/donne-e-scienza-storie-di-vita-di-alcune-delle-top-italian-women-scientists-nella-ricerca-neuroscienze-scienze-biomediche-scienze-cliniche/ |title=Donne e scienza. Storie di vita di alcune delle Top Italian Women Scientists nella ricerca Neuroscienze, Scienze Biomediche, Scienze Cliniche |date=2017 |publisher=Fondazione Onda ETS |pages=68-72 |language=it |trans-title=Women and Science. Life stories of some of the top Italian women scientists in neuroscience, biomedical sciences, and clinical sciences. |access-date=2025-11-04 |url-status=live |via=WordPress}}</ref>

==Education==

Franzini-Armstrong enrolled in the [[biological sciences]] program at the [[University of Pisa]] in 1956 and earned her [[Laurea|Laurea degree]] in 1960.<ref name="Sodowsky-8-B">{{cite journal |last1= |first1= |last2= |first2= |date= |title=Clara Franzini-armstrong profile on University of Pennsylvania website. |url=https://www.med.upenn.edu/apps/faculty/index.php/g275/p9936 |journal=Clara Franzini-Armstrong, Ph.D.}}</ref>  She became interested in [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]] after the Italian Ministry of Education gave an electron microscope to the University of Pisa.<ref name="Adler-1-B">{{cite journal |last1=Adler |first1=Elizabeth M. |date=Nov 2013 |title=Friends of Physiology: An Interview with Clara Franzini-Armstrong and Clay Armstrong |journal=The Journal of General Physiology |volume=142 |issue=5 |page=479 |doi=10.1085/jgp.201311115 |pmc=3813384 |pmid=24166877}}</ref> Franzini-Armstrong completed postdoctoral training at [[Keith R. Porter]]'s laboratory at [[Harvard University]].<ref name=Adler-1-B />
==Career==
From 1960 to 1961, Franzini-Armstrong was an assistant professor of pathology at the [[University of Pisa]]. Then, from 1963 to 1964, she worked at the National Institutes of Health with R. J. Podolsky and earned a Master of Research degree in muscle physiology.<ref name="Porter-7">{{cite journal |date=2008 |title=Porter Lecture - "From Membranes to Molecules. A Morphologist View of How Muscle Controls Calcium Movements" |url=http://comm.archive.mbl.edu/events/2008_events_friday/events_friday_07_03_08.html |journal=The Marine Biological Laboratory}}</ref> Later, from 1964 to 1966, she worked as a research assistant at [[University College London]], with [[Andrew Huxley]], where she studied contractile machinery and optical methods in Huxley’s laboratory. During this period, she also earned a second Master of Research degree in muscle structure. She worked as a research associate in physiology at [[Duke University]] in the late 1960s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marine Biological Laboratory |url=http://comm.archive.mbl.edu/events/2008_events_friday/events_friday_07_03_08.html |access-date=2025-11-04 |website=comm.archive.mbl.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Franzini-Armstrong |first=Clara |date=1970 |title=Details of the I band struture as revealed by the localization of ferritin |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0040816670800234 |journal=Tissue and Cell |language=en |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=327–338 |doi=10.1016/S0040-8166(70)80023-4|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

From 1969 to the early 1970s, Franzini-Armstrong worked as an associate in physiology at the [[University of Rochester]].<ref name="Porter-7" /> She then became an assistant professor in physiology at the University of Rochester from 1972 to 1975, before becoming an associate professor of anatomy at the University of Pennsylvania from 1975 to 1981. 

Franzini-Armstrong has been a professor emerita of cell and developmental biology at the [[Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania]] since 2007.<ref name="ClaraDepart-3" /> She and her husband are the only married couple to be members of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Kreeger-6">{{cite journal|last1=Kreeger|first1=Karen|title=Celebrating a Lifetime of Dual Career Success|journal=Penn Medicine News Blog: Archives|date=2013}}</ref>

===Research===
Franzini-Armstrong discovered that [[T-tubule]]s open at the [[Cell (biology)|cell]] surface, which helped explain how [[muscle|muscles]] contract.<ref name="Sodowsky-8-B" /> 

Franzini-Armstrong's research focuses on the organization of [[Membrane|membranes]] and [[Macromolecule|macromolecular]] complexes responsible for [[Excitation contraction coupling|excitation-contraction]] coupling in [[Cardiac muscle|cardiac]] and skeletal muscles.<ref name="College-5">{{cite journal |date=8 July 2014 |title=College of Veterinary Medicine |journal=Kansas State University}}</ref> Her structural work has been divided into four main phases: 

# The first phase focused on [[calcium]] cycling, particularly on defining the distribution and nature of the two membrane systems involved in this specific type of cycling.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shamoo |first1=Adil E. |last2=Ambudkar |first2=Indu S. |date=January 1984 |title=Regulation of calcium transport in cardiac cells |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/y84-002 |journal=Canadian Journal of Physiology and Pharmacology |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=9–22 |doi=10.1139/y84-002 |pmid=6143603 |issn=0008-4212|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
# The second phase involved identifying the location of the channels that release calcium during muscle activation. She also demonstrated that in muscles with high activity rates, a limiting factor is the density of the pump protein rather than the density of calcium release channels.<ref name="Adler-1-B" />
# The third phase identified the relationship between the [[L-type calcium channel]]s of the [[Cell membrane|plasmalemma]] and the [[T-tubule]]s in cardiac and skeletal muscles. Specifically, she worked with CaV channels, or [[Dihydropyridine receptor|dihydropyridine receptors]] (DHPRs), and the calcium release channels of the [[sarcoplasmic reticulum]] (RyRs).<ref name="Adler-1-B" />
# The fourth phase examined the [[Supramolecular chemistry|supramolecular]] complex that enables several molecules in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which regulate calcium release, to interact with one another. Franzini-Armstrong continues to employ structural approaches to better understand the various molecular interactions.<ref name="College-5" /><ref name="ClaraDepart-3">{{cite journal|title=Clara Franzini-Armstrong|journal=Department of Molecular Biology|date=2015}}</ref>

==Personal life==

Franzini-Armstrong is married to [[Clay Armstrong]], a professor of physiology at the University of Pennsylvania.<ref name=Sodowsky-8-B />

==Honors and awards==

Franzini-Armstrong's honors include a Fellowship from [[Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa|Scuola Normale Superiore]] from 1956 to 1960 in Pisa, Italy, followed by a postdoctoral fellowship (''Perfezionamento'') from 1961 to 1990.<ref name=ClaraDepart-3 /> From 1983 to 1987, she was a member of the molecular cytology study section. In 1988, she was the director of the [[Gordon Research Conferences|Gordon Research Conference]] on excitation-contraction coupling. From 1988 to 1990, she was a member of the Scientific Advisory Committee of the [[Muscular Dystrophy Association]], and a council member of the [[Biophysical Society]].<ref name=ClaraDepart-3 /> In 1989, she was the co-recipient (with Dr. Knox Chandler) of the K.C. Cole Award of the Biophysical Society. In 1990, she became the co-chairman of the Biophysical Society Symposium on Excitation-Contraction Coupling. In 1995, she was inducted into the [[National Academy of Sciences]], and in 1997, she was awarded an honorary MD from the University of Pisa. In 2001, she was inducted into the [[Royal Society|Royal Society London]] as a foreign member. She was inducted into the European Academy of Sciences in 2005, followed by the 2007 Founder's Award from the Biophysical Society.<ref name=Adler-1-B />
